Maladaptive Strategies.value: I push myself to exercise excessively

Negative Appraisals.value: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power
I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore

issues.item: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: The trauma type is trauma to a loved one, but this maladaptive strategy presumes a direct perpetrator who harmed the patient. That is hard to reconcile unless the loved one's trauma also directly involved interpersonal harm to the patient, which is not indicated here.

issues.item: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: Permanent humiliation is more characteristic of direct interpersonal victimization. With a loved-one trauma, this appraisal is not impossible, but in combination with 'others can see what happened to me' it implies a self-referential shame exposure theme that fits poorly unless the patient was also directly victimized.

vignette: Malia, a 57‑year‑old architect from a small coastal town in New Zealand, had been designing the new community center for the past year when the tragedy struck. She was returning from a site inspection when her partner, an elderly friend who had been her constant support, was struck by a van on a rain‑slicked road. The ambulance crew arrived in minutes, the air thick with antiseptic, and within hours Malia watched his life slip away in the sterile glow of the hospital corridor. The metallic tang of disinfectant and the muffled murmurs of distant patients lingered in her memory, turning any hallway or clinic room she entered into a painful reminder of that night. In the months that followed, the very spaces that once felt safe became trigger points. The antiseptic scent of any hospital or even the subtle scent of a cleaning spray in her office would flare a flash of the accident. When a client’s voice, speaking in a foreign tongue during a design review, turned into a jumble of incomprehensible chatter, Malia’s heart would pound and she would leave the meeting abruptly, stepping into the stairwell as if to escape the noise. Each of these sensory intrusions pushed her toward maladaptive coping: she began to avoid her circle of friends, declining invitations to coffee or walks, and she found herself racing through workouts at the gym, pushing her body to exhaustion as a frantic attempt to outrun the memories that the triggers invoked. The same trigger that provoked avoidance also gnawed at her sense of faith—she felt that the world had turned hostile, that people, even those closest to her, had failed to protect what she cherished. The hospital’s smell, the chaotic hum of traffic, and the foreign voices all seemed to expose her, as if strangers could read the sorrow etched into her face without a word spoken. Malia’s growing conviction that she was “exposed” to others’ judgment only deepened her retreat. She told herself that if she stayed away from friends, they would not see the way her eyes glistened or the way her hands trembled in silence. That belief, that every glance could betray the loss she carried, intensified her compulsive exercise routine. She would lace up her shoes, run past the campus track, and push her lungs to the brink, each breath a protest against the feeling that she had lost meaning in her own life. The belief that she had lost faith in people, in life, and even in a higher power, spiraled, feeding the urge to keep moving, to keep pushing, to keep proving that she was still alive and capable. The absence of meaning also sharpened her awareness of spatial triggers. Without a sense of purpose to anchor her, Malia’s mind latched onto every familiar location—a particular corner of her office, the hallway where she met clients, the parking lot where she last saw her partner’s car. Her constant vigilance turned even mundane places into potential sites of relapse, making it difficult to focus on her architectural sketches or to trust her own spatial judgments. The feeling that nothing felt meaningful anymore seemed to magnify the anxiety she felt whenever she entered a place that might echo the hospital’s sterile air or the echoing footsteps of strangers. Her compulsive exercise, a strategy that had begun as a means of control, now fed back into her negative beliefs. Each time she ran until her legs ached, she reflected on the futility of her effort, thinking that if she could not escape the memories, she could not escape the loss of faith she felt. The more she believed that her body was a battleground, the less she believed that her thoughts could heal her. Similarly, by refusing to sit for routine medical checks or to see a counselor, she reinforced the notion that medical professionals were a source of pain, a reminder of the day she watched her partner fade away. The avoidance of medical cues—ambulances passing by, the sight of stethoscopes in waiting rooms—only heightened her hypervigilance in other contexts, making her notice even the faintest suggestion of a hospital in any setting. By the time Malia stepped into a therapist’s office, the cycle was tight. Each time a familiar scent or voice rose, she fled to exercise or withdrew from social contact, which in turn deepened her sense of loss and exposed her to the world’s judgment. The fear that her friends might see her trembling, that the world had turned hostile, kept her from reaching out. Yet, the cumulative isolation had begun to erode her professional life; she found herself unable to concentrate on client briefs and began missing deadlines, which worried her colleagues and threatened her reputation. Finally, the shame of falling behind at work, coupled with the relentless internal dialogue that she was no longer in control, pushed her to seek help. She now fears that if she does not break this loop, she will lose not only her sense of faith but also the meaning she once derived from designing spaces that brought people together. She hopes that learning to reframe the triggers and to reconnect with her professional identity might restore a sense of purpose she had long felt was gone.
